questions.enonce_markdown: Examine the religiosity of Abraham and his people at the time of his call. (25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** "Religiosity" here means the religious beliefs, practices and attitudes of Abraham and of the society around him when God called him. The Book of Genesis shows a man who came from a polytheistic world and who answered a call that asked him to leave that world behind.

**1. The religious background of Abraham's family and people.** According to Genesis 11 the family of Terah lived in Ur of the Chaldees and then settled in Haran, both in Mesopotamia. Joshua 24 says that Terah and his ancestors "served other gods" beyond the river. Scholars link the religion of these cities with the worship of many gods, among them the moon god, with temples, idols, priesthoods, sacrifices and the use of household figurines. The people therefore believed that many gods controlled nature, fertility and war, and they worshipped them through images and rituals tied to a place.

**2. The religiosity of Abraham himself.** The Bible does not present Abraham as a man who already knew the one God. The call in Genesis 12 comes to him as an initiative of God ("Go from your country, your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you"). His religiosity before the call is not described, but his obedience afterwards shows a quickly growing faith. At the time of the call he was a pagan in the context of his culture, a man open to a new revelation, who obeyed without knowing the destination.

**3. The content of the call.** God promised a land, a great nation, a great name and a blessing for all the families of the earth. The call demanded a break with country, clan and household gods. This was a break with the religious and social security of the time, because in the ancient world religion was bound to the family and the land.

**4. The response of Abraham and the religious practices that follow.** Abraham left with his wife Sarah, his nephew Lot and his household. At Shechem, Bethel and Hebron he built altars and "called on the name of the Lord" (Genesis 12 and 13). He offered sacrifice, worshipped without an image and later received the covenant sealed by circumcision (Genesis 15 and 17). Faith was "reckoned to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15).

**5. His people.** Lot and the servants who followed him shared the journey and many of them were circumcised with him (Genesis 17). The surrounding Canaanites kept their own cults, and Genesis presents Abraham as a stranger and sojourner who kept his own worship, while respecting local rulers such as Melchizedek, priest of God Most High (Genesis 14).

**Conclusion.** At the time of his call Abraham and his people lived in a polytheistic, idol-using culture. Abraham's religiosity is shown not by what he already knew but by his obedient and trusting response, which began a new relationship with one God and the covenant on which Israel's faith was built.
